Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

('2024-06-20 09:19:23.499691+00:00', '65e0e94f-36d8-f3a7-039e-c1770857c3ce', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

"Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

('2024-06-20 09:40:00.407711+00:00', '65e0e94f-36d8-f3a7-039e-c1770857c3ce', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures 1. Locate the process that is related to the alert. Inspect parent processes and why they were launched.
2. Take note of the name of the remote device and the command that might have been executed.
3. Verify the unusual system activity with system owners.​
4. Check files for prevalence, their locations, and digital signatures.​
5. Check the timeline of both the devices for other suspicious activities around the time of the alert.
6. Submit relevant files for deep analysis and review file behaviors. ​

B. Scope the incident.
1. Find related alerts and activities on both devices. Find out whether they are part of a wider incident in the incident graph.
2. Identify unexpected processes, check suspicious files for prevalence, location and digital signature, submit for deep analysis to inspect behaviors.
3. Identify communications to devices, network addresses, and domains. Verify unusual activities with device owners. Check reputation of URLs and websites.

C. Contain and mitigate the breach.
1. If activity on any of the involved devices is unexpected, isolate the device to prevent the threat from progressing.

('2024-06-20 09:40:00.275880+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', Subsequent analysis revealed command and control behavior of malware which was blocked.
question_dict.question: What was the URL associated with the command and control behavior detected in the end alert?

Suspicious remote activity was observed on the account `dp5hn`.
Command and Control behavior was blocked for the URL `http://vectorsandarrows.com/`.

Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures That data is likely in AlertEvidence (ThreatFamily or Categories fields) and tied to devices via DeviceId/DeviceName; then I can map to AadDeviceId via DeviceInfo. I’ll search AlertEvidence for entries mentioning CommandAndControl, then map any associated device to its AadDeviceId, excluding vnevado-win10s.

Action: execute[
SELECT 
  ae.TimeGenerated,
  ae.AlertId,
  ae.Title,
  ae.Categories,
  ae.ThreatFamily,
  ae.DeviceName,
  ae.DeviceId
FROM AlertEvidence ae
WHERE 
  ae.ThreatFamily LIKE '%CommandAndControl%'
   OR ae.Categories LIKE '%CommandAndControl%'
   OR ae.Title LIKE '%CommandAndControl%';
]

To find “the IP address from which the ransomware payload was remotely launched,” I need to pivot from these process/file activities to:
- Network telemetry (DeviceNetworkEvents: RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine), and/or
- File-origin metadata (DeviceFileEvents: FileOriginIP, RequestSourceIP),
and tie that to the ransomware executable.

First, I’ll:
1) Identify any “ransomware” detections tied to these events in AlertEvidence (ThreatFamily, RemoteIP).
2) If that’s not enough, I’ll pivot on the same devices and time window (around 2024‑06‑20 09:10–09:40) in DeviceNetworkEvents and DeviceFileEvents to find suspicious connections or file-origin IPs, then pick out the IP associated with the ransomware binary.

Action: execute[
SELECT TimeGenerated,
       AlertId,
       Title,
       ThreatFamily,
       DeviceName,
       ProcessCommandLine,
       RemoteIP,
       RemoteUrl,
       FileName,
       FolderPath
FROM AlertEvidence
WHERE (ThreatFamily LIKE '%ransom%' OR Title LIKE '%ransom%' OR AttackTechniques LIKE '%ransom%')
   OR (ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%vssblatemp.exe%' OR ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%get-userprttoken.ps1%' OR ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%bcdedit /set bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures%')
ORDER BY TimeGenerated
LIMIT 200;
]

       FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields
FROM AlertEvidence
LIMIT 20;

-- 2) Look for any AlertEvidence mentioning PRT or Primary Refresh Token
SELECT TimeGenerated, AlertId, DeviceName, DeviceId, Title, Categories, AttackTechniques,
       FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields
FROM AlertEvidence
WHERE Title LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%' 
   OR Title LIKE '%PRT%' 
   OR Categories LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%' 
   OR Categories LIKE '%PRT%' 
   OR AttackTechniques LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%' 
   OR AttackTechniques LIKE '%PRT%' 
   OR AdditionalFields LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%' 
   OR AdditionalFields LIKE '%PRT%'
ORDER BY TimeGenerated;

-- 3) Look for any evidence tied to the given device ID, regardless of date
SELECT TimeGenerated, AlertId, DeviceName, DeviceId, Title, Categories, AttackTechniques,
       FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields
FROM AlertEvidence
WHERE DeviceId LIKE '%e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033%'
   OR DeviceName = 'vnevado-win11t'
ORDER BY TimeGenerated;
]

('2024-06-20 09:19:23.690415+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

•	Find the infection source and block it (IP or email)
•	Rebuild the affected machine.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. CommandAndControl detections appear on multiple hosts (vnevado-win10s, vnevado-win10r, vnevado-win11t, vnevado-win11u). I’ll first inspect SecurityIncident to find any incident referencing Manatee Tempest or vectorsandarrows.com, then look at related alerts/evidence and the involved hosts.

SELECT *
FROM SecurityIncident
WHERE Title LIKE '%Manatee Tempest%' 
   OR Title LIKE '%vectorsandarrows.com%' 
   OR Description LIKE '%Manatee Tempest%' 
   OR Description LIKE '%vectorsandarrows.com%'
LIMIT 20;
]

The question asks specifically for the host where CommandAndControl malware was detected during lateral movement. In the Manatee Tempest pattern, the incident starts with initial access on vnevado-win10r, then spreads (lateral movement) to other devices. Since vnevado-win10r is the initial-access host, the lateral-movement phase would be detections on a different host that was subsequently compromised. Among the listed hosts, vnevado-win10s has CommandAndControl detections and is distinct from the initial host, so it represents a lateral movement target. Therefore, the host name we need is the full device name for that lateral-movement detection.

You are a security analyst. 
You need to answer a given security question by querying the database.
The logs are stored in a MySQL database, you can use SQL queries to retrieve entries as needed.
Note there are more than 20 tables in the database, so you may need to explore the schema or check example entries to understand the database structure.

Your response should always be a thought-action pair:
Thought: <your reasoning>
Action: <your SQL query>

In Thought, you can analyse and reason about the current situation, 
Action can be one of the following: 
(1) execute[<your query>], which executes the SQL query
(2) submit[<your answer>], which is the final answer to the question

As part of the process leading to the discovery of an unknown malware, we found that components such as `cmd.exe`, `mimikatz.exe`, and `notepad.exe` were executed to conduct unwanted malicious activities. While the investigation revealed that an alert was raised due to the detection of this malware, the machine should still be thoroughly examined to rule out any possible infection. Relating to this incident, a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected. Can you identify the file name of the process involved in this attempt?

Thought: I need to understand the database structure and find where alerts related to PRT access attempts are stored. I’ll start by listing all tables to identify where security alerts, process executions, or malware detections are logged.

Action: execute[SHOW TABLES;]

[('AADManagedIdentitySignInLogs',), ('AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs',), ('AADProvisioningLogs',), ('AADRiskyUsers',), ('AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs',), ('AADUserRiskEvents',), ('AlertEvidence',), ('AlertInfo',), ('AuditLogs',), ('AzureMetrics',), ('CloudAppEvents',), ('DeviceEvents',), ('DeviceFileCertificateInfo',), ('DeviceFileEvents',), ('DeviceImageLoadEvents',), ('DeviceInfo',), ('DeviceLogonEvents',), ('DeviceNetworkEvents',), ('DeviceNetworkInfo',), ('DeviceProcessEvents',), ('DeviceRegistryEvents',), ('EmailAttachmentInfo',), ('EmailEvents',), ('EmailUrlInfo',), ('Heartbeat',), ('IdentityDirectoryEvents',), ('IdentityLogonEvents',), ('IdentityQueryEvents',), ('MicrosoftAzureBastionAuditLogs',), ('MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs',), ('SecurityAlert',), ('SecurityIncident',), ('SigninLogs',), ('ThreatIntelligenceIndicator',), ('UrlClickEvents',), ('Usage',)]

Thought: I need to locate the specific alert or related telemetry about a Primary Refresh Token (PRT) access attempt and then identify which process/file was involved. Likely candidates are SecurityAlert, AlertEvidence, and DeviceProcessEvents. I’ll first search SecurityAlert for anything mentioning “Primary Refresh Token” or “PRT” to find the relevant alert, then pivot to the evidence/process table.

Action: execute[
SELECT *
FROM SecurityAlert
WHERE Title LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%'
   OR Title LIKE '%PRT%'
   OR Description LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%'
   OR Description LIKE '%PRT%'
LIMIT 50;
]
ProgrammingError: Unknown column 'Title' in 'where clause'

Thought: The previous query failed because I assumed column names that don’t exist. I need to inspect the structure of the SecurityAlert table to see which fields contain the alert title/description, then search for PRT-related alerts.

Action: execute[DESCRIBE SecurityAlert;]

[('TenantId', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('TimeGenerated', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('DisplayName', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('AlertName', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('AlertSeverity', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('Description', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('ProviderName', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('VendorName', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('VendorOriginalId', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('SystemAlertId', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('ResourceId', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('SourceComputerId', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('AlertType', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('ConfidenceLevel', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('ConfidenceScore', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('IsIncident', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('StartTime', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('EndTime', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('ProcessingEndTime', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('RemediationSteps', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('ExtendedProperties', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('Entities', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('SourceSystem', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('WorkspaceSubscriptionId', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('WorkspaceResourceGroup', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('ExtendedLinks', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('ProductName', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('ProductComponentName', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('AlertLink', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('Status', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('CompromisedEntity', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('Tactics', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('Techniques', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('SubTechniques', 'text', 'YES', '', None, ''), ('Type', 'text', 'YES', '', None, '')]

Thought: Now that I know the column names in SecurityAlert, I should search its AlertName, DisplayName, and Description fields for references to “Primary Refresh Token” or “PRT” to find the relevant alert. After that, I will pivot to AlertEvidence (and possibly DeviceProcessEvents) to identify the process/file involved in that PRT access attempt.

Action: execute[
SELECT SystemAlertId, AlertName, DisplayName, Description, TimeGenerated
FROM SecurityAlert
WHERE AlertName      LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%'
   OR AlertName      LIKE '%PRT%'
   OR DisplayName    LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%'
   OR DisplayName    LIKE '%PRT%'
   OR Description    LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%'
   OR Description    LIKE '%PRT%'
ORDER BY TimeGenerated DESC
LIMIT 50;
]

[('b9665560-3146-cb1d-2325-4985ae787d78', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

The logs are stored in a MySQL database, you can use SQL queries to retrieve entries as needed.
Note there are more than 20 tables in the database, so you may need to explore the schema or check example entries to understand the database structure.

Your response should always be a thought-action pair:
Thought: <your reasoning>
Action: <your SQL query>

In Thought, you can analyse and reason about the current situation, 
Action can be one of the following: 
(1) execute[<your query>], which executes the SQL query
(2) submit[<your answer>], which is the final answer to the question

A security incident involving the deletion of all file snapshots and shadow copies via WMI or VSSAdmin, which is common during ransomware infection, was detected. The process `vssblatemp.exe` with process ID 1900 was used to perform the deletion. This incident might be part of a larger malicious campaign as described in the Activity Profile: Iranian MOIS operators opportunistically deploy limited-impact wiper in response to Israel-Hamas war. Following this alert, we also detected malicious command and control behavior. Can you provide the URL associated with this command and control behavior?

It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. A security incident involving ransomware-like behavior impacting several devices has been observed. Initial detection included the use of PsExec to launch a command on a remote device, suggesting lateral movement using this tool. This was followed by suspicious activities leading to compromised assets exhibiting ransomware-like behavior. The attacker might be using the specified user account, IP, or device to infect multiple devices with ransomware. Automated remediation actions were considered to address the threat. What is the name of the file that is associated with the ransomware-like behavior?

Thought: I need to identify which table(s) contain information about ransomware-like behavior, PsExec usage, or automated remediation, then find the specific file name tied to that ransomware behavior. I’ll start by listing all tables in the database to understand the schema.

Action: execute[SHOW TABLES;]

[('AADManagedIdentitySignInLogs',), ('AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs',), ('AADProvisioningLogs',), ('AADRiskyUsers',), ('AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs',), ('AADUserRiskEvents',), ('AlertEvidence',), ('AlertInfo',), ('AuditLogs',), ('AzureMetrics',), ('CloudAppEvents',), ('DeviceEvents',), ('DeviceFileCertificateInfo',), ('DeviceFileEvents',), ('DeviceImageLoadEvents',), ('DeviceInfo',), ('DeviceLogonEvents',), ('DeviceNetworkEvents',), ('DeviceNetworkInfo',), ('DeviceProcessEvents',), ('DeviceRegistryEvents',), ('EmailAttachmentInfo',), ('EmailEvents',), ('EmailUrlInfo',), ('Heartbeat',), ('IdentityDirectoryEvents',), ('IdentityLogonEvents',), ('IdentityQueryEvents',), ('MicrosoftAzureBastionAuditLogs',), ('MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs',), ('SecurityAlert',), ('SecurityIncident',), ('SigninLogs',), ('ThreatIntelligenceIndicator',), ('UrlClickEvents',), ('Usage',)]

Thought: I need to find which alert or incident describes this ransomware-like behavior with PsExec and then determine the file name associated with it. Likely relevant tables are:
- SecurityAlert / SecurityIncident (overall descriptions)
- AlertEvidence (entities/files tied to alerts)
- DeviceFileEvents (file activity on endpoints)

First I’ll search SecurityAlert for records mentioning “ransomware” and/or “PsExec” to identify the relevant alert(s), then pivot into AlertEvidence or DeviceFileEvents to get the file name.

Action: execute[
SELECT TimeGenerated, AlertId, AlertName, Description
FROM SecurityAlert
WHERE Description LIKE '%ransomware%'
   OR AlertName LIKE '%ransomware%'
   OR Description LIKE '%PsExec%'
   OR AlertName LIKE '%PsExec%'
ORDER BY TimeGenerated DESC
LIMIT 50;
]

From that alert, I can then pivot (likely via AlertEvidence or the Entities/ExtendedProperties fields) back to the specific process in DeviceProcessEvents, but first I must locate the correct alert.

Action: execute[
SELECT
  TimeGenerated,
  AlertName,
  DisplayName,
  Description,
  SystemAlertId,
  Entities,
  ExtendedProperties
FROM SecurityAlert
WHERE AlertName LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%'
   OR AlertName LIKE '%PRT%'
   OR Description LIKE '%Primary Refresh Token%'
   OR Description LIKE '%PRT%'
ORDER BY TimeGenerated DESC
LIMIT 20;
]

Thought: I have identified several "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)" alerts in the SecurityAlert table. Each alert’s Entities JSON includes the process tree. I now need to determine which specific alert is associated with the broader ransomware-like incident involving files get-userprttoken.ps1, characterical.zip, characterical.zip.lockbit, IP 99.83.111.100, and user S-0-6-5, then extract the process ID and command line for the process that attempted to access the PRT. However, in the PRT alerts I inspected, the relevant process is consistently BrowserCore.exe launched by PowerShell running get-userprttoken.ps1. The question asks specifically: “What is the process ID and command line of the process that was used in the possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT)?” In the alert details, the “affected process” is the BrowserCore.exe instance, not the parent PowerShell. For the alert example corresponding to get-userprttoken.ps1, the Entities field clearly shows:
- ProcessId: 1640
- CommandLine: "browsercore.exe"
So the answer is that BrowserCore.exe process with PID 1640 and command line "browsercore.exe" was used in the possible PRT access attempt.

Action: submit[The process used in the possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was:

- Process ID: 1640
- Command line: "browsercore.exe"]
